newsitem.title: UK: Oil up then down as stocks data sends mixed message.
newsitem.headline: Oil up then down as stocks data sends mixed message.

text.p: World oil prices rose on Wednesday in response to bullish heating oil stock data from the United States, but later fell as traders turned their attention to growing gasoline inventories.
A modest early recovery from a series of seven consecutive days' losses was seen by some traders as heralding a period of relative stability for the market.
But benchmark December Brent crude fell again in late trade to close three cents lower at $22.16 a barrel on the London futures market.
"Short term the market looks a little oversupplied ...but generally demand is buoyant," said Russell Hill, senior trader at Austrian oil company OMV.
Both the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported a surprise drop in U.S. distillate stocks in the week ending November 1.
But they also showed a fairly sharp rise in crude stocks and a substantial build in gasoline stocks.

EIA data released on Wednesday showed U.S. distillate stocks fell 500,000 barrels last week and the API data, issued after the market close on Tuesday, pegged the drop at 429,000 barrels. Analysts had expected a build of some 2.5 million barrels.
But API data showed a 4.7 million barrel increase in gasoline stocks, while the EIA estimated the build to be 2.7 million barrels.
Within the distillate category, key heating oil inventories in fact rose - but by less than dealers had expected, helping to underpin an earlier rally in heating oil and crude values.
Traders also noted that heating oil stocks were still well down on year-ago levels.

Low heating oil stocks in the run-up to the peak northern hemisphere winter demand period were one of the main factors behind the blistering rally in oil to a six-year peak of $25.06 per barrel in mid-October.
But mild weather, a recovery in heating oil stocks and investment fund selling helped wipe over 10 percent off the price of a barrel of oil.
While another cold snap would aid any recovery, the highs may not be broken for some time, some analysts said.
"I am fairly friendly to this market, but I am less confident of taking out the 1996 high this year," Hill said.
